speakeroldname: Hon. H. S. BELAND (Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-estabilishment):
speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is not much change in this vote. There were eight employees last year, there are six this year, the supervisor of expenditures and the head clerk having been dispensed
11 p.m. with, which accounts for the reduction in the vote. The reason that the civil government vote has always been presented in this way is, I think, that originally it was intended ,to mention only the permanent staff, and it does not in any degree reflect the number of employees of the department.

How many employees are
covered by the item?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Page 102 gives the details: One deputy minister; one assistant deputy minister; one assistant secretary and chief Clerk; one principal clerk; one storekeeper; one departmental! librarian. In addition there is an allowance of $600 for a private secretary.

I do not want to be
charged with reflecting on any of these civil servants, but would the minister tell me how many deputy ministers lare in his two departments, Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment and Health?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: There is a deputy minister in each department.

Again I do not want to be charged with any reflection on these gentlemen, but we have before us a vote for $6,000 for a deputy .minister of this department and another vote of $5,000 for an assistant deputy minister. No doubt they are competent and

Supply

Re-establishn-ent

capable officials, but they preside over a staff of only four. Does it not look to be just a trifle top-heavy, $11,000 for two first class, highly trained, competent -men to preside over so small a staff? Frankly, I think the time has arrived when we must look that fact in the faice.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I am very glad, Mr. Chairman, that my hon. friend has asked the question. The number of employees in the department is not 6; it is 2,422.
That is very nice. That is the number in this particular branch?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Yes. I have endeavoured to explain that originally, under the former administration, only six or perhaps a few more, perhaps ten or twelve in all, were mentioned in the civil government estimates, the reason being that the large majority, practically the totality of the members of the department, some 8,000, were only temporary employees. They have been reduced in number very considerably year after year. During the former administration the number of employees was reduced in some years by over 1,000, perhaps 1,600; three yeare ago the number was reduced by 1,000, and two years ago by some 700 or 800. Last year again, the number was reduced by 600, or thereabouts. The number of employees still drawing salary in the department is 2,422.
What does that include?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
It includes all the employees in the administrative work, all the employees in the Vet Craft shops, all the employees in the limb factory, all the employees and doctors in the hospitals of the department, all the physicians who are employed full-time outside of the hospitals for pension examination, and so forth. In a word, it includes all the employees of the department. The number of these employees on the 1st January, 1924, speaking from memory, was 2,922. On the 1st of April last, the number was 2,422, so that during thirteen months, continuing the reduction process which had been started, the number of employees had been reduced by 500.
Perhaps this w7ould be a proper occasion to set right some opinion which has been expressed as regards the cost of administration of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment. Speaking personally, I have not the remotest desire to be in charge of the department one day longer than I am desired, but I must say that the work which is new being discharged in Canada in connection with this depa:tment will be maintained for a large number of years to come, and the num-

ber of employees engaged in the work of the department will be reduced by a smaller margin as the years go by. The time will come, I should say within five or six or perhaps ten years, when you will not be able for a long number of years thereafter to reduce the number any further. And why? Because the department has the whole administration of pensions, which involves the paying out in one year of $34,000,000. It would be a simple matter to pay $34,000,000 to one man, but it is an altogether different thing when you have to pay pensions to 64,000 different people every month, and when a large number of those pensioners are not permanent in their disability, thousands of them in the course of one year being either reduced, cancelled or increased, thousands of new pensions being awarded during one year, and hundreds, if not thousands, of children being bom to pensioners and who have also to be taken into account. That is one feature of the work.
But there is another feature, and that is the paying of pensions to Imperials in Canada. The amount that is being paid on account of the Imperial government to Imperial pensioners in Canada is around $10,000,000. The department is acting in Canada for the Imperial government in regard to these pensioners.
Is not that a large increase? Last year it was only $7,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Yes, there is a large increase.
To what is the increase due?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: That includes also the pay and allowances which are paid to Imperial pensioners who are under treatment in Canada.

Is this $10,000,000 of
Imperial pensions included in the $34,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
No, it is in addition to
that.

Do the Imperial authorities
pay the cost of administering those pensions.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: They do. We are reimbursed, but we have to provide the money in the first place. -We have a section in the department which is called the Imperial section, there being 105 employees in that section alone.

The increase in
Imperial pensions seems enormous. Are there more Imperial pensioners coming out?

Supply-Re-establishment

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Perhaps there are. I can
give later on when we consider the item for pensions the exact number of Imperial pensioners in Canada last year and this year. Now I am just making a general statement.
Is the Dominion government reimbursed by the Imperial for both the Imperial pensions and the cost of administering those pensions?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Yes. I want only to set
at rest the minds of my hon. friends on the other side; for instance, the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) and the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling), whose presentation 1 very much admired the other day. I did not care to interrupt the hon. gentleman, 'but he went so far as to say, unintentionally and unwittingly, I am quite sure, that 71 per cent of the amount of money which is voted for this department goes into administration expenses. If it were true, if half of this were true, if only one-quarter of it were true, I would be the first man to be scandalized. As my hon. friend from York-Sunbury has said himself, it would indeed be scandalous. But what is the situation in this connection? I appeal to my hon. friend from Yale not to stake his reputation on the statement he made in this connection, because it is absolutely inaccurate. What is the total amount involved in this department in one year? It is $51,000,000, and every cent of it is administered by the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. Now how did my hon. friend contrive to arrive at the figure that 71 per cent of $51,000,000, or whatever it is, has been expended in administration? My hon. friend said that only a small share of that money goes direct to the men; the balance of it is expended for salaries and administration. Now what are the facts? I ask the question without any idea of creating the impression that my hon. friend has been misleading the House. I do not think it was his intention; nor do I think it was the intention of any newspaper man who publishes such broad and unwarranted statements; but it is time-it may be late in the day; perhaps it should have been done long ago-that this matter should be explained fully to hon. members. Let us take the amount which goes directly to the men in cash. In the first place the sum of $33,048,000 is paid in pensions. This is money that goes to the men or to their dependents without the omission of one cent. The balance left from that $51,000,000 would be about $18,000,000. How is that made up? In round figures the sum of $4,463,000 is paid 201J
to tihe Imperials either in pension or in pay and allowances. Is there anything else being paid to the men in cash? Surely. What else? Pay and allowances to the men who are being treated in hospitals. The men who are admitted into hospital for treatment receive not only shelter, clothing, food, and medical care but they receive also pay and allowances. But the amount paid to the men under treatment varies according to whether the man is single or whether he has a wife or a wife and children. The amount of pay and allowances is $2,314,044.59. This money is paid in cash to the men or their dependents. There are also pay and allowances made under a certain order in council and the total of the two classes of payment is $2,816,000.
That figure does not agree with the vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: My hon. friend does not take into consideration other allowances, smaller in character, which help to make up the total. The hon. gentleman may accept my word that the pay and allowances amount to $2,816,000. Add the $33,000,000 odd for pensions to Canadians, or to the dependents of those men, and the $4,463,000 paid to the Imperial pensioners in pensions and pay and allowances. There are still other sums that go to the men in cash. We must consider the salaries that are paid to the men in the craft shops under the jurisdiction of the department; they must be paid because they are suffering from disabilities that do not permit them to seek employment elsewhere. We have three or four hundred of these men employed by the department in shops and these men draw their salaries in cash. Now let us take insurance. The department administers a soldier's insurance which is not a very considerable branch.
Before the minister passes to the subject of insurance, can he tell us what the administration expenses are for the payment of all the pensions?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Yes, I am coming to that; I will be pleased to give my hon. friend those figures.

The minister
did not state how much is paid for salaries in the craft shops?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
In wages to operators
$95,822. Now let us take vocational loans, that is to say the loans made to the men who have completed a course of vocational training under the department and who secure a loan from us in cash for the purchase of
Supply-Re-establnhment

equipment. The money thus paid to them in cash for the year 1923-24 was $37,893. The war service gratuity is also money paid to the men in cash. Now we come to the returned soldier's insurance-

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: It is a small amount,

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: It is, yes. Now on account of the deaths of soldiers who carried insurance with the department we paid out during the same year $241,887 in death benefits; $203,704 in annuities; and $917 in disability benefits. Then there must be considered cash surrender values, return of premiums, and so on, making a total paid in cash to the men in connection with returned soldiers' insurance of $483,000. Surely not a single one of the amounts I have mentioned can be claimed as money spent for administration. Out of the total of $41,000,000 odd that I have mentioned there is not a single cent which is not paid directly to the men.
Would the minister be good enough to give us the figures for the amounts paid to disabled men who are in the employ of the department, in their own shops? He has overlooked that figure.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Yes, they correspond closely with the figures for that year.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
We had a supplementary
estimate that year which probably accounts for the difference. The hon. member is referring to the main estimates.

of last year are before us.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I refer to the year 1923-24. That is the statement I have. But they coincide pretty well from year to year. Now let us consider another point. In addition to this amount which is paid in cash to the men or their dependents a large amount of
[Mr. BSland.j
money is paid for services rendered to the men. For example: We have the item of medical attendance upon soldiers who require an operation, or who require any medical treatment. I ask any hon. member in this House, in all sincerity, is that money which is being expended for attendance on a soldier in a hospital not equivalent to money which is paid to him direct? It is for a service which is of benefit to the men; and if you handed the money to the man himself he would employ it for that very service. Are the services of nurses attending our soldiers not to be considered as equivalent to a direct payment, inasmuch as if we handed the money to the men they would pay for the services of the nurses? I will go one step further. Is not the money which is being spent and paid to experts, skilled workmen, to make limbs for the thousand amputation cases which we have in Canada equivalent to the money paid to the men themselves? If we supplied the money to the amputation cases what would they do with it but provide artificial limbs? I quote these as examples. We have a large number of medical men in Canada employed in this department. I have the figure here and I will give it later. These men are not employed for administration purposes, except in very few instances, but they are employed for the purpose of rendering certain services to the men, which is equivalent to paying the money to the men themselves. What is the amount of money which is being used for those services? It is $5,648,118.

Which item of
the estimates is that under?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I agree with my hon. friend, but I have attempted to point out that under the item of salaries is included the salaries of all these parties I have referred to, all the physicians in the hospitals, all the physicians outside the hospitals engaged in the examination of pensioners all over Canada, probably 30,000 disabled pensioners, who are examined under the instructions of the board every six months. Then we have the nurses, the staffs in the hospitals, orderlies and so on. The item for salaries covers them all. So that I say, Mr. Chairman, it was an unhappy reference by, I think, my hon. friend from Yale (Mr. Stirling) the other day. I do not think the hon. member has given this matter the proper attention and perhaps he was led into making the statement because he had read something in the newspapers about it. But those are the conditions. That the staff should have been reduced every year as the years went by was conceded by everybody, and the staff was reduced year by year to a large extent. Since I have been in the department I have no doubt we have reduced the number of employees by over 3,000. We have reduced the number in the course of the last year, plus one month, by 500, and I pray hon. members to note that a large proportion of these employees are returned men themselves and in many cases disabled soldiers. It is always a difficult task for any minister to retire an employee in a department such as this. It is perhaps an easy task for my hon.
colleagues to retire officials, but it is painful to be obliged to retire men who have-seen service and suffered disability, who-have wives and families, and who are receiving a salary of $1,200, $1,500 or $1,800. It is not agreeable. It would not be agreeable to any man. We take all necessary precautions in these reductions of staffs. We notify the man beforehand; we give him two or three months' notice, and we provide for the payment of two months' salary after retirement. If a man, who has been a faithful servant, but who is surplus, finds that after two months he is unable to secure employment, and if he claims that he should have one more month in order to attempt to secure a job somewhere else, we allow it. But administer it in any way you like, it is a painful and difficult task, and I do not think you could decrease the number by more than fifty a month at the best. That is what we have been doing. I have given this explanation because it was due to hon. members. I am quite certain that in many minds the idea prevails that at least fifty per cent of the money voted in the House of Commons for the soldiers was money that went for administration expenses. That is absolutely beside the mark. The department does not claim perfection. The department has been administered by men of ability, regardless of who was the head under the previous administration or under this administration, by men who have seen service overseas, everyone of whom, with barely one or two exceptions, has seen honourable service in France. It is only due to them that we should tell the House that they are working every minute of their time, and to my personal knowledge, after hours fifteen days in a month. The situation cannot be otherwise because, when you retire in one week ten or twelve people, they were doing something. While perhaps they were not doing a day's work, you have to load other employees with the work, and they have to go back to their office after five, or six or seven o'clock in the evening in order to acquaint themselves with the new work that has been placed in their care.
The idea has prevailed that the medical staff is too large. I have myself many times felt that, perhaps, we should be able to reduce the number of physicians whom we employ in our hospitals. I look at Christie street in Toronto where there is a large hospital with five or six hundred patients, patients who come in and patients who go out, some who remain for two, three or four years and some who remain for one month or two or three months. We have a large staff of medical men there. But that is not all. Not only are the medical
Supply-Re-establishment

men working in the hospitals, but they are administering what we call clinical treatments to hundreds at Christie street hospital. I have seen that mysallf. I wanted to satisfy myself that such was the condition. Last year we administered more than 160,000 different dlinioal treatments. When a soldier comes into a hospital or the unit-it is the same place now in Toronto because we have contracted the service and everything is now under one roof-seeking treatment, it is impossible to say to that man: You are looking for treatment; you cannot have it; you have to go out; you will) not be attended to. That mian must be admitted and you must have a physician examine him. His case may require services of a specialist or, perhaps, two or three specialists. This is now about seven years after the war. A disability that has been recurrent after two, three, four, five or six years may be very much complicated, and it may require an X-ray man to take radiographs of this man's body. It may require a surgeon to ascertain that an operation is not needed. Heaven knows that we make mistakes, especially in the medical profession. It is too well known that in many oases the diagnosis is not made as it might be; but, as the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Ross) knows that is the weak side of our profession, and unhappily amongst our medical men there are some who make mistakes like the rest of us. You have to examine this man; you have to delcide whether he requires treatment or not, and you have to admit him to hospital or to refuse him. Alii that requires services, and nobody will give you those services for nothing, especially if it is the government that requires the services. It is my expectation that the number of employees will be further reduced in the course of the present year by a few hundred and probably next year also, although the number of patients is about the same as it was twelve months ago. When we are on this item "care of patients", I might explain that last year we Laid in our hospitals, I think 3,730 patients, and the last figure I 'have of patients under treatment is 3,704, or only a few less than last year. It is sometimes claimed that the department is too severe, that our medical men are refusing treatment to people who are entitled to treatment. I do not know whether this accusation is well founded or not, but at all events I have never heard that the medioal men in the employ of the department have allowed into the hospitals patients who should not be allowed. I do not know of any man who is being treated to-day who does not deserve treatment. It may be that some may claim that a few soldiers are not being treated '
who are entitled to treatment. In the last instance we have to abide by medical opinion, because this is largely a matter of medical appreciation. I am sorry that I have detained the committee so long, but I thought it was only fair that I should give hon. members this explanation.

I asked the minister during
his remarks to state the cost of the administration of pensions. He said that he would give me the figures, but he has not done so. I would like to draw the attention of the committee to one point in connection with a statement made by the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling), who does not happen to be in his seat at the moment. That hon. member did not refer to the amount that is being expended for pensions nor to the cost of administration for pensions. My impression has always been that the cost of administration for pensions is comparatively small. The hon. member for Yale was referring to an entirely different matter. He was distinguishing between the cost of administering pensions exclusively, and the other branch of soldiers' civil re-establishment, and if any statement has been made which is not correct the hon. member for Yale will be only too glad to see it corrected. I invite the minister now to give a concise statement of the cost of administering pensions as distinguished from soldiers' civil re-establishment.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
There is no information
available on the question. There is no proper administration of the pensions except that which is being carried out by the department; there is no administration of pensions outside the department.

Is there no information
available to enable the minister in the future to tell us how much it costs to administer pensions to the extent of $34,000,000 annually?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
It would be very involved
accounting work, although it might be done. The hon. member will bear in mind that the employees who administer the allowances to the men in hospitals also administer pensions. We have only one department under one roof in Ottawa; all these employees are at their desks and do whatever work of administration is required of them. At one time pensions were administered by a pension board entirely outside of the department; that was previous to 1921. It was my immediate predecessor who combined both the administration of pensions and that of the re-establishment department proper. At the time that was done about 800 employees were

Supply-Re-establishment
transferred from the Board of Pension Commissioners to the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment and the amount of money paid for the administration of the pensions by these 800 employees was some $880,000. That is the only information available. It may be that after many years of practice and training on the part of the employees the amount would be much smaller if the administration of the pensions were entirely in the hands of a separate board; but at the time of the merging of the two branches there were transferred to the department proper, as I have said, some 800 employees.

The way the
estimates are prepared invites the kind of comparison which the minister complains of.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I grant you that.

There is nothing whatever in the vote for the soldiers' civil re-establishment, on its face, to show that there is anything in it having regard to pensions, while on the other hand item 94 provides for salaries and contingent expenses of the Board of Pension Commissioners for Canada. Under the heading of pensions we are paying $109,380 in salaries. It is obvious therefore that anyone taking up the government's figures must work out the same result and come to the same kind of mistake, if it is a mistake, as did the hon. member for Yale.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Item 94 has no reference at all to administration; the amount of $89,000 as'-ed for covers the salaries of the immediate personal staff and ten medical advisers. I grant you that, placed as these figures are in the estimates, my hon. friend from Yale might have been misled; but he should not have been misled to the extent of saying that 71 per cent was going into administration. That was absolutely beyond the mark. But if the item for pensions were placed with the estimates of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, it would be seen immediately that the amount paid out in administration in this department can compare favourably with the cost of any other department in the government or of any business corporation in Canada. At any rate, not being a business man myself, that is the information I have received from an accountant of experience whom I asked to give me the real situation.

Now, the minister graciously told us that he did not want to hold the committee. It is now ten minutes to twelve; can he not let us go? I make this suggestion with certain feelings of commiseration for the minister; I dislike to see all the government's pre-election statements going by the board one after another. I dislike to see the promise in regard to eleven o'clock adjournments being broken.

That is not a pre-election
statement.

If we are unable to rely on the pre-election statements of the government, at least we might be pardoned for assuming that we have some right to rely on their statements made since we have been in this House. I suggest that we might pass this item and adjourn.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Surely, after all my exertion in giving the long explanation I did to the committee, an explanation rendered unavoidable by reason of the statements made by the member behind my hon. friend, he will reward me by allowing a larger item to pass. I was expecting that the whole estimates of the department would be adopted to-night; I have given a long explanation and supplied a good deal of information.

I made a very
fair proposition to my hon. friend. We will let the item go through and adjourn.

On this item, we
have been so far discussing matters relating to something else. While I have little to say about this particular vote I shall have a good deal to say on some other items. There are certain items on pages 22 and 23, and on page 56 again we have votes for soldiers' civil re-establishment. Some of these subjects I should like to deal with.

Let us adopt a few items
to show that we want to make some progress.

I think the minister has
had enough experience of members on this side of the House to know that we wish to do everything to facilitate these matters, but it is most unreasonable for him to expect us at this late hour to go into these items in an intelligent manner, and in fact it is unfair to the soldiers to attempt it.
